chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Taxation can make a big difference in the real return of an income property. Well understood, it reduces your tax legally; ignored, it holds unpleasant surprises.

This guide presents the main principles: how rental income is taxed, deductible expenses, depreciation, capital gains on resale, and the question of holding personally vs through a corporation.

Informational content, not tax advice: every situation differs, consult an accountant or tax specialist. Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: Rental income and deductible expenses
chapters.objective: Understand what is taxed and what is deductible.
chapters.html:
Understand what is taxed and what is deductible.

Rental income is taxable, but you deduct the expenses incurred to earn that income. The net income (rents minus deductible expenses) is added to your taxable income.

  • Deductible: mortgage interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance and repairs, management, common-area energy, etc.
  • Key distinction: a repair (immediately deductible) vs an improvement (a capital expenditure, depreciable).
  • Keep all your invoices and maintain rigorous records.
Emilie's tip

Keep clean books from day one. Every invoice kept is a potential deduction; every deduction forgotten is tax paid needlessly.

chapters.title: Depreciation (CCA)
chapters.objective: Understand this powerful tool… and its pitfalls.
chapters.html:
Understand this powerful tool… and its pitfalls.

The capital cost allowance (CCA) lets you deduct part of the building's value (not the land) each year, reducing your taxable income. It is a powerful tool, but a double-edged one.

On resale, the depreciation claimed can be « recaptured » and taxed. Depreciation therefore defers tax more than it eliminates it: use it strategically, ideally on the advice of a tax specialist.

Emilie's tip

Depreciation is not « free » tax savings: it is often deferred tax. Use it knowingly, with an accountant's advice, according to your time horizon.

chapters.title: Capital gains on resale
chapters.objective: Anticipate the tax on the gain.
chapters.html:
Anticipate the tax on the gain.

When you resell a rental building at a profit, part of the gain (the capital gain) is taxable. A rental building does not benefit from the principal-residence exemption (except for the portion you occupy, if any).

Planning (timing of the sale, ownership structure, carried-forward losses) can influence the tax. Here again, a tax specialist is a worthwhile investment.

Emilie's tip

Plan the taxation of the resale BEFORE you sell. The timing and manner of the sale can significantly change the tax on your gain.

chapters.title: Personal ownership or through a corporation
chapters.objective: Choose the right structure for your project.
chapters.html:
Choose the right structure for your project.

You can hold a building in your personal name or through a corporation (incorporation). Each option has tax, legal, and financing implications. Incorporation can offer advantages (protection, planning) but also added costs and complexity.

The right choice depends on the size of your project, your time horizon, and your overall situation. It is a decision to make with an accountant and a notary/lawyer.

Emilie's tip

Don't incorporate « by default » or « because you heard it somewhere ». For a first building, personal ownership is often simpler; incorporation makes sense as the portfolio grows.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Set up rigorous record-keeping.
  2. List my deductible expenses.

Within 30 days

  1. Consult an accountant about depreciation and the ownership structure.
  2. Plan my medium-term tax strategy.

Then

  1. Review the planning before any resale.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Net rental income: rents minus deductible expenses, taxable.
  • Repair vs improvement: immediately deductible vs a capital expenditure.
  • CCA (depreciation): a deduction on the building, with recapture on resale.
  • Capital gain: the taxable gain on the resale of a rental property.
  • Incorporation: ownership through a corporation, with advantages and costs.
